A run already going when another is picked finishes with the harness it started with, and a conversation is only carried on by the harness it began with; the next request with another harness starts a new one.
Each harness is run its own way, streaming what it does as a line of JSON per event, which is read into the same reply, tool calls, usage, and result, whichever harness wrote it:

- Claude Code is `claude -p`, in auto mode, the system prompt given with `--append-system-prompt`, a conversation carried on with `--resume`, and a copy of one with `--fork-session`.
- Codex is `codex exec`, with `--full-auto` and `--json`, the prompt read from its standard input, a conversation carried on with `resume`.
- OpenCode is `opencode run`, with `--format json`, a conversation carried on with `--session`.

Codex and OpenCode take no system prompt of their own, so it is given ahead of the prompt, marked off from it. Neither can carry on a copy of a conversation, so a question asked while another is running starts a new conversation with them instead. The notes, commit messages, and prompt titles are written with a small model where the harness can be told one, Claude Code's haiku, and with the harness's default model otherwise.
When the harness picked isn't installed, a run on the host fails saying that it can't be run, as any run that can't be started does. A run in a container uses the harness in its image instead, and fails, where Podman isn't installed or can't run, as the [ContainerEnvironmentScope](../container-environment/index.md#container-environment-scope) says.

#### Protected Locations

Only a run on the host has protected locations. A run in a container has none, since nothing it mustn't touch is mounted there, as the [ContainerEnvironmentScope](../container-environment/index.md#container-environment-scope) says: it isn't guarded, and its harness is given no rule against reading or editing anything.
Where the harness takes rules for what its tools may do, as Claude Code does with `--disallowedTools`, a run on the host is told what its mode keeps it off. A Code task is told it may not edit the spec location, and a Spec task the code location; the application puts back whatever changes there all the same, and says so in the task's output as a passive notice, never an error, as the [TaskTableScope](../../ui/components/task-table/index.md#task-table-scope) says. A Code task is also told it may not read the spec location, alongside that, so it reads the compiled reference instead, as the [ModeSystemPromptsScope](../prompt-mode/mode-system-prompts/index.md#mode-system-prompts-scope) says. A question from the Ask tab always runs in a container, so it is never given this rule, nor any other telling it to keep off the spec location. This rule is only a nudge, and doesn't enforce anything, since a shell command can still read the files, and nothing puts anything back or stops the run when one does. A harness that takes no such rules is told nothing of either.

#### Feeding

A task's run is given its prompt as a stream of messages: Claude Code with `--input-format stream-json`, each message written as a line of JSON on the harness's standard input, which stays open for as long as the run lasts. The run's first message is the task's compiled prompt, as ever, and each message sent to the task after it, from the [ChatInputScope](../prompt-mode/chat-input/index.md#chat-input-scope), is written as another.
A message reaches the harness when it finishes what it is doing rather than interrupting it, so a run that is mid-tool-call takes it once that call is over. The harness echoes each message back as it takes it in, with `--replay-user-messages`. A message taken in between turns is answered with a result of its own, and one taken while a turn is under way is answered within that turn, sharing its result.
A run can also start work in the background that goes on after its turn ends: Claude Code's subagents, shell commands run in the background, such as a long build, and any other kind of background task it adds later. Every such task holds the run open, whatever its kind. The run keeps each background task that has started and not yet ended, by its id: one starts when the harness says a task has started, and ends when the harness notifies that task's end, whatever it ended as. A notification doesn't say what kind of task it is, so it is matched by id against those seen starting. The harness wakes the run when a background task ends, so it can act on what came of it.
A result no longer ends the task on its own. The run's last result is the first to come once every message sent has been taken in and no background task is still going. A result that comes before then, while a message sent hasn't been taken in or a background task is still going, is only an answer: the task keeps running, its input stays open, and more can still be sent to it. At the last result the run's input is closed, but the task is only shown as finished once the harness's process has exited as well, and it then finishes in the state of that last result; until the process exits, the task keeps running. A process that exits without a last result finishes the task as a run with no result does, failed. A run that is stopped closes its input and ends straight away, whatever is still going in the background, since its whole process group is ended with it.
Codex's `codex exec` and OpenCode's `opencode run` read a single prompt and can't be fed more while they work, so a task running with either takes its prompt as ever and can't be sent more.
Questions, the palette's file search, the one-off runs, and the notes, commit messages, and prompt titles each take a single prompt, as ever.

#### Images

Images attached to a prompt, as the [ChatInputScope](../prompt-mode/chat-input/index.md#chat-input-scope) says, are given to the harness as it takes them: to Claude Code as image content blocks, base64-encoded with their media type, in the same stream-json user message as the prompt's text, after it; to Codex with an `--image` argument per image; and to OpenCode with a `--file` argument per image. A message fed to a running Claude Code task carries its images the same way, and a Claude Code run that isn't fed more but has images is given its prompt as a stream-json message too, so the images can go with it. Codex's options end with `--` before the prompt when it is given images. Questions take images as tasks do.

#### Context

The harness keeps its context between requests instead of starting fresh each time. Each lane of the [PromptSendingScope](../prompt-mode/sending/index.md#prompt-sending-scope) carries on a conversation of its own, so nothing a task of one lane read reaches a task of the other: the spec lane's, carried on by Spec tasks and a Chain prompt's spec steps, and the code lane's, carried on by Code tasks, a Chain prompt's code step, and Freeform tasks. Each task sent carries on its own lane's, and since a lane runs one task at a time, two tasks never carry on the same conversation at once. A Chain prompt's steps hand on to each other as text, the prompt and what the step before replied, as the [ModeSystemPromptsScope](../prompt-mode/mode-system-prompts/index.md#mode-system-prompts-scope) says, so the handoff crosses lanes whatever each lane's conversation holds. When the project is opened, each lane carries on the latest conversation among its own tasks in the history, a Chain task by the lane of the step it was.
The spec lane and the questions always run in a container, and the code lane always on the host, so each conversation is only ever carried on where it began. A run in a container keeps its conversation's sessions in the project, in its own folder of `.suspense/sessions/`, as the [ContainerEnvironmentScope](../container-environment/index.md#container-environment-scope) says, so it carries on across runs, restarts of the application, and moves of the project; a run on the host keeps them where the harness keeps them on the host.
Questions from the Ask tab share a separate conversation of their own, and when the project is opened they carry on the latest conversation among the questions saved with it. A question asked while another is running carries on a copy of that conversation, so questions running at the same time never write over each other. A conversation is only carried on in the project it began in, each open project keeping its own tasks' and questions' conversations while it is in the background. A spec lane or questions conversation from before its sessions were kept in the project, whose session the project's sessions folder doesn't hold, is still tried, and when the harness has no such session, the request is sent again at once as a new conversation, as below.
A request whose conversation can't be carried on, because the harness says it has no such session, as Claude Code's "No conversation found", or because it was begun elsewhere, is never failed for it, and never retried on the same conversation: it is sent again at once as a new conversation, the same prompt, with no context, and the conversation it couldn't carry on is not tried again by any later request, the project's history included. A question sent again so is recorded and shown as starting a new conversation, as the [AskConversationScope](../prompt-mode/ask-conversation/index.md#ask-conversation-scope) marks one. Each run applies its own prompt's systemPrompt, even when it carries on a conversation begun in a different mode. The palette's file search always starts fresh.
A conversation can be left for a new one, from the chat input's New conversation button, as the [ChatInputScope](../prompt-mode/chat-input/index.md#chat-input-scope) says, which leaves the conversation of the lane it is used for: the next request in it starts a new conversation with no context, and the one left is not carried on again, not by a run of it still going, nor by the project's history. Leaving it is kept with the project, as the [ProjectDataScope](../project-data/index.md#project-data-scope) says, so a project opened after a lane's or the questions' conversation was left starts a new one there too, rather than carrying on the latest conversation in its history, until a run after the reset begins one of its own. How much context a conversation holds is known from what the harness reports with each reply: everything the model was given, cached or not, and what it wrote, as of its latest reply; replies of subagents don't count.

#### Failures

A run that fails always says what went wrong, in the harness's own words, which are the error its result carries, or the error events it streamed, and where it gave none, what it printed on its standard error, and its exit status, as written. A task shows it in its output and a question at the end of its answer. It never reads only "the harness reported an error", or any other message that leaves the cause unnamed; a generic line is only ever a heading above what the harness said. A run that couldn't be started says why it couldn't, and one Podman couldn't run says so, as the [ContainerEnvironmentScope](../container-environment/index.md#container-environment-scope) says.

#### Baked Prompts

[BakedSystemPromptsScope](./baked-prompts/index.md#baked-system-prompts-scope)

#### One Off Runs

[OneOffAgentRunScope](./one-off-run/index.md#one-off-agent-run-scope)

#### Catalog

[HarnessCatalogScope](./catalog/index.md#harness-catalog-scope)

#### Mode System Prompts

[ModeSystemPromptsScope](../prompt-mode/mode-system-prompts/index.md#mode-system-prompts-scope)

# Running Activity Scope

## Concept

### Pitch

What the application is still working on, where to see it and get back to it, and what makes quitting ask first.

### Shape

#### Description

What counts as work still running in the application, and how each is listed, newest last.

#### Running

- each task the harness is working on, from the [PromptEditor](../prompt-mode/index.md#prompt-editor), one in each lane at most, headed "Task" with the first line of its prompt
- each question still running, from the [ChatInputScope](../prompt-mode/chat-input/index.md#chat-input-scope)'s Ask tab, headed "Question" with its first line
- a spec build run on its own, as the [SpecBuildScope](../spec-build/index.md#spec-build-scope) says, "Building the spec"
- a divergence analysis in the [DivergenceScope](../divergence/index.md#divergence-scope), "Analyzing divergence"
- a search for concepts to rescope in the [RescopeScope](../rescope/index.md#rescope-scope), "Finding scopes to extract"
- a run target of the [RunTargetsScope](../run-targets/index.md#run-targets-scope) running, "Running" then its name, or its targets being found, "Finding how to run"

Prompts waiting in the queue don't count as running, since they are saved with the project, and neither does a panel whose work is over.
Everything running counts in every open project of the [OpenProjectsScope](../open-projects/index.md#open-projects-scope), not only the one on screen. Those of the project on screen come first, then each other project's, its rows headed with that project's folder name after the kind, such as "Task · my-project".

#### Indicator

While anything is running, a small spinner shows, with how many things are running beside it when more than one is. Its tooltip says what is running, or how many things are. While nothing is, neither shows, and nothing takes their place. Where it sits is up to what holds it.

#### List

Clicking the spinner opens a small list beneath it of everything running, one row each, in the order above, each with a small spinner of its own. Clicking a row closes the list and reveals what it is, first switching to its project when it belongs to another:

- the latest task brings back its output, closing the previous tasks and any inset panel over it, and scrolls it to the end; a task running in the other lane, among the previous tasks, expands the previous tasks and opens it there
- a question selects the chat input's Ask tab and closes any inset panel, scrolling the Ask conversation to it
- a divergence analysis, a rescope search, or a run target brings its [MinimizablePanelScope](../../ui/components/minimizable-panel/index.md#minimizable-panel-scope) back
- a spec build has nothing to show, so its row only closes the list

Pressing the mouse outside the list, or <Escape>, closes it too, as does everything in it finishing.

#### Quitting

Quitting, however it is asked for, while the harness is working on a task or a question, or while a spec build runs on its own, in any open project, asks first. A divergence analysis, a rescope search, or a run target doesn't ask, and quitting stops it. The message is titled "Quit while a task is running?" and says what is still running: the harness working on a prompt, piton build, or both, and, when it runs in more than one project, in how many projects. "Quit" exits, and "Keep Running" or <Escape> dismisses it. Asking to quit again while it is open doesn't open a second one, and an open palette closes first.
----
# Right Sidebar Scope

## How To Build

A RightSidebarScope should be built as a reusable component that will be reused throughout the rest of the codebase.  A component is configurable through arguments or properties that alter its behaviour, appearance, and details.  A RightSidebarScope should encapsulate all of its own reusable behaviour, while leaving the wiring, intergration, and integration to the domain of the application.

## Theme

Drawn in the [ThemeScope](../../theme/index.md#theme-scope): its surfaces, text, lines, accent, and status colours are the theme's roles, named as the theme names them, in both dark and light mode, never colours of its own.

## Side

right

## Width

260

## Min Width

160

## Panels

- [ReferencedFilesPanel](./referenced-files/index.md#referenced-files-panel)
- [UnderstandingPanel](./understanding/index.md#understanding-panel)
- [SubagentsPanel](./subagents/index.md#subagents-panel)

## Sidebar

It runs along the right of what it sits beside, with a thin line down its left edge, where the two meet. It is resized by dragging that edge: it starts 260 pixels wide and can't be dragged narrower than 160.
It holds its panels one above the other, in the order it lists them, each across its full width. A single thin line, in the theme's line colour, lies between one panel and the next, never two, unless the next panel says its own change of colour is the edge. A panel that isn't shown for the moment takes no room and leaves no line.
It is on the theme's base surface, as its panels' bodies are.

## Concept

### Pitch

A second [SidebarScope](../sidebar/index.md#sidebar-scope), at the right of the message list and the chat input beneath it, that lists the spec files the running task references, so it's clear what part of the spec the harness is working from, and the constraints it has taken from it for the task.

### Shape

#### Description

It runs the full height of the body, beside the body's tab bar, the message list or file beneath it, and the chat input beneath those, which stops at its left edge rather than running beneath it. It keeps the width it was dragged to while the application runs.
Its panels sit one above the other, in this order: the referenced files at the top, the understanding beneath them, and the subagents last, along the bottom of the sidebar, beneath both. The referenced files are only as tall as their rows need, up to half the sidebar's height, scrolling beyond that; the subagents, once there are any, are only as tall as their rows need, up to 30% of the sidebar's height; and the understanding fills what is left between them, until they are resized. While the run has started no subagent, the understanding reaches the sidebar's bottom.

#### Resizing Panels

The panels themselves can be resized, as the sidebar can. The edge between one panel and the next, where the lower panel's header meets the body of the one above, is a handle: dragging it up or down moves that edge, the panel above growing as the one below shrinks, or the other way, their contents laid out anew at each height as it changes. Hovering the handle shows the resize cursor for up and down and a thin line along the edge in the theme's accent, which goes once the pointer leaves and the drag is over; otherwise no line is drawn there, the change of colour still being the edge.
No panel can be dragged shorter than its header and one row of its contents, 32 pixels below its header, nor can one be pushed out of the sidebar. Once a panel has been dragged, it keeps its height rather than being only as tall as its rows need: the referenced files no longer fit their rows or stop at half the sidebar, and scroll once their rows are taller than the height they were given. The heights they were dragged to are kept while the application runs, the next time the sidebar slides out included, as its width is; when the sidebar's height changes, as when the window is resized, the referenced files and the subagents keep their heights and the understanding takes what is left, as far as the smallest heights allow. Double-clicking the handle puts both panels back as they start, the referenced files fitting their rows again.

#### Look

The sidebar's body is on the ribbon's command area colour, #222222 in dark mode. Each panel's header is 32 pixels tall, on the darkest surface, #111111 in dark mode, as the file tree is, its title in small semibold text, 8 pixels from the left, with no count beside it. There is no line anywhere in it, not between a header and its body, nor between one panel and the next: the change of colour is the edge. Each header has, along its bottom, the 1 pixel border in its panel body's colour that every panel header has, as the [SidebarScope](../sidebar/index.md#sidebar-scope) says, which is no line, since it is the body's own colour. The only line is the one down its left edge, where it meets the message list and the chat input, which is the handle it is resized by, apart from the line that shows along the edge between two panels while it is hovered or dragged, as resizing the panels says. In light mode the same steps are taken, as the ribbon's are.
Neither panel has a permanent scrollbar, since its column would break the 8 pixel inset: a panel shows its scrollbar only while its contents are taller than it, and none otherwise. When it shows, it is the same scrollbar as every other, as the [ScrollbarScope](../scrollbar/index.md#scrollbar-scope) says.
A panel whose contents fit doesn't scroll at all, not even by a pixel, at any display scale or window size: it counts as taller than its contents need only once they overflow it by a whole pixel or more, so what is left over from rounding to the display's pixels never counts, and while they fit, it stays scrolled to its top. So neither the wheel nor a drag moves rows that all fit, and no scrollbar shows for them.

#### Showing

It is only there while a task is running: from the moment a task is sent from the Code, Chain, or Spec tab until its run is over. Questions from the Ask tab never show it, even when one is sent from the queue.
When a task starts, it slides out from the right edge of the message list and the chat input, growing from nothing to its width, its contents sliding into view from behind that edge as it does. When the run is over, it slides back the same way. The slide is quick and settles without bouncing. It pushes rather than covers: from the first frame of the slide to the last, the body's tab bar, the message list or open file beneath it, and the chat input end exactly at the sidebar's left edge, narrowing as it grows and widening as it shrinks, laid out again each frame, as the [BodyScope](../../../scope/application/Body.md#body-scope) says. Nothing runs beneath the sliding sidebar, nothing is clipped by it, and nothing jumps to a new width once the slide settles.
----

#### Resizing Panels

The panels themselves can be resized, as the sidebar can. The edge between one panel and the next, where the lower panel's header meets the body of the one above, is a handle: dragging it up or down moves that edge, the panel above growing as the one below shrinks, or the other way, their contents laid out anew at each height as it changes. Hovering the handle shows the resize cursor for up and down and a thin line along the edge in the theme's accent, which goes once the pointer leaves and the drag is over; otherwise no line is drawn there, the change of colour still being the edge.
No panel can be dragged shorter than its header and one row of its contents, 32 pixels below its header, nor can one be pushed out of the sidebar. Once a panel has been dragged, it keeps its height rather than being only as tall as its rows need: the referenced files no longer fit their rows or stop at half the sidebar, and scroll once their rows are taller than the height they were given. The heights they were dragged to are kept while the application runs, the next time the sidebar slides out included, as its width is; when the sidebar's height changes, as when the window is resized, the referenced files and the subagents keep their heights and the understanding takes what is left, as far as the smallest heights allow. Double-clicking the handle puts both panels back as they start, the referenced files fitting their rows again.

#### Look

The sidebar's body is on the ribbon's command area colour, #222222 in dark mode. Each panel's header is 32 pixels tall, on the darkest surface, #111111 in dark mode, as the file tree is, its title in small semibold text, 8 pixels from the left, with no count beside it. There is no line anywhere in it, not between a header and its body, nor between one panel and the next: the change of colour is the edge. Each header has, along its bottom, the 1 pixel border in its panel body's colour that every panel header has, as the [SidebarScope](../sidebar/index.md#sidebar-scope) says, which is no line, since it is the body's own colour. The only line is the one down its left edge, where it meets the message list and the chat input, which is the handle it is resized by, apart from the line that shows along the edge between two panels while it is hovered or dragged, as resizing the panels says. In light mode the same steps are taken, as the ribbon's are.
Neither panel has a permanent scrollbar, since its column would break the 8 pixel inset: a panel shows its scrollbar only while its contents are taller than it, and none otherwise. When it shows, it is the same scrollbar as every other, as the [ScrollbarScope](../scrollbar/index.md#scrollbar-scope) says.
A panel whose contents fit doesn't scroll at all, not even by a pixel, at any display scale or window size: it counts as taller than its contents need only once they overflow it by a whole pixel or more, so what is left over from rounding to the display's pixels never counts, and while they fit, it stays scrolled to its top. So neither the wheel nor a drag moves rows that all fit, and no scrollbar shows for them.

#### Showing

It is only there while a task is running: from the moment a task is sent from the Code, Chain, or Spec tab until its run is over. Questions from the Ask tab never show it, even when one is sent from the queue.
When a task starts, it slides out from the right edge of the message list and the chat input, growing from nothing to its width, its contents sliding into view from behind that edge as it does. When the run is over, it slides back the same way. The slide is quick and settles without bouncing. It pushes rather than covers: from the first frame of the slide to the last, the body's tab bar, the message list or open file beneath it, and the chat input end exactly at the sidebar's left edge, narrowing as it grows and widening as it shrinks, laid out again each frame, as the [BodyScope](../../../scope/application/Body.md#body-scope) says. Nothing runs beneath the sliding sidebar, nothing is clipped by it, and nothing jumps to a new width once the slide settles.

# Task Table Scope

## How To Build

A TaskTableScope should be built as a reusable component that will be reused throughout the rest of the codebase.  A component is configurable through arguments or properties that alter its behaviour, appearance, and details.  A TaskTableScope should encapsulate all of its own reusable behaviour, while leaving the wiring, intergration, and integration to the domain of the application.

## Theme

Drawn in the [ThemeScope](../../theme/index.md#theme-scope): its surfaces, text, lines, accent, and status colours are the theme's roles, named as the theme names them, in both dark and light mode, never colours of its own.

## Columns

Type, Output, and Status

## Lock

each use

## Collapses

step

## Pitch

A table of rows under a header of named columns, that can grow long and keep growing while it is shown, and stays smooth however long it gets.

## Table

Its header reads Type, Output, and Status.
Each use says whether its table has the lock to the bottom, and whether it starts on.
A use can say its table collapses its steps, which the first row counts as "Show 1 step" or "Show N steps".

## Concept

### Pitch

The output of one run of the harness, as a table of everything it did, filling in as it does it.

### Shape

#### Description

A [TableScope](../table/TableScope.md#table-scope) with Type, Output, and Status columns, with one row per thing the harness did, in order: each piece of reply text, each tool call, and any error. It is the same table wherever a run's output is shown, a task, a previous task, the palette's search for a file, or a run in one of the application's own panels, and each use says where it sits. The answers to questions are the exception: they read as chat replies, as the Ask conversation says.

#### Types

##### Description

Type is a coloured badge with an icon. Reply text is "Reply", errors are "Error", a notice from the application about the run, as its notices say, is "Notice", and a message sent to the run while it works is "Sent". Tool calls are "Files" for Read, Glob, Grep, LS, and NotebookRead; "Edit" for Edit, MultiEdit, Write, and NotebookEdit; "Command" for Bash, BashOutput, KillShell, and KillBash; "Web" for WebFetch and WebSearch; "Agent" for Task and Agent; and "Tool" for anything else.

#### Status

##### Description

A tool call's status is "running", "done", "failed", or "cancelled", and a call still running when the run ends takes the state the run ended in, "cancelled" for a run that was cancelled.

#### Replies

##### Description

Reply text is rendered as markdown, with no border around it. What subagents do is left out. If nothing streamed but the harness reports a final result, that result is shown as the reply. A finished run with nothing to show reads "No output."

#### Outcome

##### Description

Once a run is over, its final summary is headed by a row of small tags saying what the run did, so what came of any prompt, a task or a question, can be told at a glance. The final summary is the reply text the run gave after its last tool call, or the final result shown in its place; the tags head the last row of that text. They sit above the row's text, in its Output cell, with a little room beneath them, left to right in the order below, wrapping onto another line if the cell is too narrow. Each is a small label in extra small text, with a little padding either side and slightly rounded corners, 4 pixels from the next. A run that gave no reply text after its last tool call, such as one that failed or was cancelled before it gave one, shows its tags on its last row instead, whatever that row is.

##### Tags

Each tag is shown only when it applies, worked out from what the run did, not from what it was asked or what it said:

- "Wrote spec", in Spec's colour, when it wrote or edited a file in the spec location, as the [ProjectLocationsScope](../../../scope/project-locations/index.md#project-locations-scope) says, or under .claude/reference
- "Wrote code", in Code's colour, when it wrote or edited a file in the code location, the project config's codeRoot
- "Wrote files", in the theme's muted grey, when it wrote or edited a file in neither, outside the project's own data in .suspense
- "Answered", in Ask's colour, when it wrote or edited no file at all, or only files in .suspense, and gave a final summary, as a question almost always does
- "No changes", in the theme's muted grey, when it wrote or edited no such file and gave no final summary

So a run shows one or more of the first three, or exactly one of the last two. The spec location is the one the task was sent against, as its compiled prompt records, or for a run that doesn't record one, the project config's root; a project whose config gives no codeRoot has no code location, and nothing counts as code in it.
A file counts as written or edited when the run's tool calls report writing or editing it, with a file tool or a shell command, as the referenced spec works them out, a subagent's included; a file only read never counts. Each colour is its mode's, as the [PromptModesScope](../../../scope/prompt-mode/modes/index.md#prompt-modes-scope) colours it, including any colour chosen in the theme editor. The label is in the colour at full strength, on a faint tint of it, about a sixth of its strength, readable in light and dark mode.

##### Not While Running

While the run is under way, no tags are shown; they appear once it is over, however it ended, done, failed, or cancelled. A task or question restored from the history, among the previous tasks or answers, shows them as its record replays, worked out against the project it belongs to, the same as when it ran.

#### Tool Calls

##### Description

A tool call's Output cell shows its most telling argument. For Files, Edit, Command, Web, and Agent calls the tool's name is left out, since the badge already says what it is; any other tool's name comes first. Arguments other than commands are shown on a single line.

##### Paths

Any path inside the project directory is shown relative to it, and the project directory itself reads `.`.

##### Commands

A command is shown whole, as a syntax-highlighted bash block, and a long one is split across lines at `&&`, `||`, `|`, and `;`, one command per line with the chained ones indented. It never splits inside quotes, command substitutions, brackets, comments, or heredocs.

#### Streaming

##### Description

While the run is under way, the table ends in a waiting row for whatever the harness does next. As soon as a row's type is known, its badge is real, and as soon as its text or argument arrives, that is shown.

##### Raw Output

Until a row has something meaningful to show, its Type cell is a skeleton and its Output cell shows the last three lines of the harness's raw JSON output: muted, monospace, JSON syntax-highlighted, and always three lines tall so the row doesn't jump. Before any output has arrived it reads "Waiting for the harness…".

##### Skeletons

While the input of a Files, Edit, Command, Web, or Agent call is still arriving, its Output cell shows only a skeleton.
A skeleton stands in for a running row only while there is nothing meaningful to show for it. As soon as there is, no skeleton is shown for it at all.

#### Scrolling

##### Description

The table usually has its lock to the bottom, following the run's latest output. While the end of the table is scrolled out of view, raw output that would only change the waiting row redraws nothing. What a row shows that never changes once known, such as a command laid out across lines or a line of raw output highlighted, is worked out once.

#### Collapsed Steps

##### Description

A use can say its table collapses the steps leading up to the answer, once the run is finished, as the [TableScope](../table/TableScope.md#table-scope) collapses rows. The steps are every row up to and including the harness's last tool call; the answer is the rows after it.
A run with no tool calls, or with nothing after its last one, has nothing to collapse and shows whole. A run still under way shows its latest step as usual.

#### Sent

##### Description

A run can be sent more while it works. Each message sent to it is a row of its own, in order among what the harness did, where it was sent. Its Type is a "Sent" badge, and its Output the message's first line, the whole message as it was typed shown on hover. The rows after it are what the harness did in answer, until the next message. A Sent row has no status.
A Sent row is never collapsed among the steps leading up to an answer.

#### Notices

##### Description

A notice is something the application tells the run's reader about the run, rather than something the harness did or a failure: chiefly that it put back changes a task made where its mode may not change anything, a Code task in the spec or a Spec task in the code. It is passive. It is never shown as an error, never in the theme's error colour, and never fails the task, changes its status, or counts among the errors a run ended with.

##### Row

A notice is a row of its own, where it happened among the run's rows, its badge reading "Notice" with an info icon, in the muted grey of a badge that marks nothing wrong. Its output is a single line summing it up, muted, beside a right chevron, such as "Put back 3 spec files this Code task changed" or "Put back 1 code file this Spec task changed". It has no status.

##### Details

Clicking the line expands the notice's details in place, beneath it, and its chevron turns down; clicking it again collapses them. For changes put back, the details say that a task in its mode may not change that location, so what it changed there was put back as it was, and then list each file put back, one per line, by its path in the project. A notice starts collapsed, and each stays as it was left for as long as the application runs.

##### Kept

A notice is kept with its task, and shown the same wherever the task's output is, the latest task's table, a previous task opened, and a Freeform or Ask reply read as a chat, where it sits among the reply's steps as a muted line that expands the same way, never at the reply's end with its errors.

#### Legibility

The output from a realtime agent should be readable and meaningful.

#### Narrow Widths

However narrow the table is drawn, the Output column keeps most of its width. The Type and Status columns are no wider than their widest label needs, and the space inside the cells and around the table tightens as the table narrows, so the output is never squeezed into a sliver between padding and empty space.

#### Resending

A prompt sent before can be sent again, from a Resend button: a small ghost button with a rotating-arrow icon, whose tooltip says it sends the prompt again as it was sent. It sits at the right of the latest task's header, and of the heading of each previous task and previous answer, beside its chevron; clicking it never opens or closes the item.
Resending sends the prompt as it was typed, in the mode it was sent in, with the text that was attached to it, and sliced or not as it was, as though it were sent afresh from the chat input: a task queues while its lane is busy, a question runs straight away, and either is compiled anew, against the spec and system prompt as they are now, building the spec first as any task does, and saved in the history as a new task or question. The prompt resent stays where it is. A prompt whose mode isn't known, saved before modes were, is resent from the chat input's selected tab. What is being written in the chat input, and attached to it, is left alone, and so is the Slice toggle.

#### Cancelling

A task under way can be cancelled, from a Cancel button: a small ghost button with a stop icon, whose tooltip says "Cancel this task", at the right of the latest task's header, beside its Resend button, shown only while the task is building, compiling, or running. With a task running in each lane, the one that isn't the latest task shows among the previous tasks as Running, with the same Cancel button at the right of its heading, beside its Resend button, and clicking it never opens or closes the item. A task is cancelled straight away, whatever the harness is in the middle of: a build or compile under way is abandoned before the task is run, and a run is stopped, the harness's process ended, not left to finish its turn.
A cancelled task keeps the output it had so far, and its status reads "Cancelled", as the [MessageList](../message-list/index.md#message-list) shows, in the history as much as in its header. It adds no commit note, and any change the harness had already made to files is left as it is. Its lane's queue carries on after it, as it does after a task that fails, sending the next prompt waiting in it, and the next task carries on the same conversation. The task in the other lane, and questions, are not cancelled with it.

#### Sending To The Other Mode

A task sent in Code alone can be sent to Spec, and one sent in Spec alone can be sent to Code, from a small ghost button beside its Resend button, tinted the colour of the mode it sends to, whose tooltip says "Send to Spec" or "Send to Code". It sits wherever Resend does for a task, at the right of the latest task's header and of the heading of each previous task, and clicking it never opens or closes the item. Tasks sent in Chain, questions, and prompts whose mode isn't known don't offer it.
Sending to the other mode is resending, as above, in every way but the

# Message List

## How To Build

A MessageList should be built as a reusable component that will be reused throughout the rest of the codebase.  A component is configurable through arguments or properties that alter its behaviour, appearance, and details.  A MessageList should encapsulate all of its own reusable behaviour, while leaving the wiring, intergration, and integration to the domain of the application.

## Theme

Drawn in the [ThemeScope](../../../ui/theme/index.md#theme-scope): its surfaces, text, lines, accent, and status colours are the theme's roles, named as the theme names them, in both dark and light mode, never colours of its own.

## Concept

### Pitch

The task view of prompt mode: the tasks sent to the harness and their output as the harness works on them.

### Shape

#### Description

Shows tasks and their output, not a conversation. Prompts aren't shown on the right with responses on the left, and tool calls aren't gathered into groups. Freeform is the exception: a Freeform task is shown as a regular chat, as its freeform says.

#### Sent Prompt

##### Description

A task's header shows the compiled markdown that was actually sent to the harness, rendered as markdown, once it has compiled, along with the name of the hidden anchor it was compiled from.

#### Status

##### Description

A task's status is a coloured label that spells it out: "Building" in blue, "Compiling" in cyan, "Running" in yellow, "Done" in green, "Failed" in red, "Cancelled" in orange, and "Not recorded" in grey for a task from the history with no record of its run. The labels are readable in both light and dark mode.

#### Output Table

##### Description

A task's output is a [TaskTableScope](../../../ui/components/task-table/index.md#task-table-scope), whose rows are what the harness did for the task. While the task is under way, its table ends in the waiting row for whatever the harness does next. Tasks never collapse their steps, since their whole chain is of interest.

#### Links

##### Description

Links in the compiled prompt and in reply text are clickable. A link to a file opens it, as the [OpenFileScope](../../open-file/index.md#open-file-scope) says, and a web link opens in the browser. The file path on a Read, Edit, Write, or MultiEdit row is shown as a link and opens that file the same way.

#### Backgrounds

##### Description

use /lib
use /ui
use /ui/components/sidebar/Panel
from .. import RightSidebarScope
from /scope/harness-integration import HarnessIntegrationScope
from /scope/prompt-mode/modes import PromptModesScope

export panel SubagentsPanel:
    title: Subagents
    counted: false
    height: fit
    scrolls: true
    scrollbar: overflowing

    concept: {SubagentsConcept}

concept SubagentsConcept:
    pitch:
        The bottom panel of the @{RightSidebarScope}, beneath the referenced
        files and the understanding: the subagents the harness started for
        the running task, each shown in the colour of the mode that started
        it.

    shape: {SubagentsShape}

shape SubagentsShape:
    description:
        It lists only subagents, the agents the harness started, never the
        other background tasks a run starts, such as shell commands run in the
        background, which hold the run open, as the
        @{HarnessIntegrationScope} says, but aren't shown here.

        It is shown only once the run has started a subagent, and takes no
        room before. One row per subagent, in the order they started, each 24
        pixels tall, 8 pixels in from the panel's edges: a spinner while it is
        at work, then a tick, a cross, or a dash for how it ended, done,
        failed, or stopped, beside what it was started to do, in small text,
        cut off with an ellipsis, muted once it has ended. Its tooltip gives
        what it was started to do, and beneath, muted, its kind and what it
        is doing or how it ended. The panel is only as tall as its rows need,
        up to 30% of the sidebar's height, scrolling beyond that.

    byMode:
        Each subagent is shown according to the mode of the task that started
        it, as the @{PromptModesScope} colours modes: its row has a bar 2
        pixels wide down its left edge in that mode's colour, and its spinner
        and tick are drawn in it too, while a cross or dash keeps its own
        colour. A subagent's mode is the mode its task was sent in, and for a
        step of a chain, the step's own: the spec step and a spec follow-up
        are Spec's, and the code step is Code's, never Chain's purple. Its
        tooltip names the mode, "Started by the Code task", "Started by the
        Spec step", and so on. A task whose mode isn't known, as one from the
        history saved before modes were, has no bar and keeps its spinner and
        tick in their own colours, its tooltip reading "Started by the task".
        A Chain task on its own, before its code step has been sent, is the
        chain's spec step, so its subagents are Spec's and labelled "Spec".

        While a chain runs, the panel keeps the subagents of each of its
        steps, not only the step running: they are grouped by step, in the
        order the steps ran, each group headed by a small label in its mode's
        colour, "Spec", "Code", or "Spec follow-up", with the step running
        last. A task that isn't part of a chain has one group, and no label.
        Once the run is over, the sidebar slides back with them all, as it
        says.
----

with `--replay-user-messages`. A message taken in between turns is
        answered with a result of its own, and one taken while a turn is under
        way is answered within that turn, sharing its result.

        A run can also start work in the background that goes on after its
        turn ends: Claude Code's subagents, shell commands run in the
        background, such as a long build, and any other kind of background
        task it adds later. Every such task holds the run open, whatever its
        kind. The run keeps each background task that has started and not yet
        ended, by its id: one starts when the harness says a task has started,
        and ends when the harness notifies that task's end, whatever it ended
        as. A notification doesn't say what kind of task it is, so it is
        matched by id against those seen starting. The harness wakes the run
        when a background task ends, so it can act on what came of it.

        A result no longer ends the task on its own. The run's last result is
        the first to come once every message sent has been taken in and no
        background task is still going. A result that comes before then, while
        a message sent hasn't been taken in or a background task is still
        going, is only an answer: the task keeps running, its input stays
        open, and more can still be sent to it. At the last result the run's
        input is closed, but the task is only shown as finished once the
        harness's process has exited as well, and it then finishes in the
        state of that last result; until the process exits, the task keeps
        running. A process that exits without a last result finishes the task
        as a run with no result does, failed. A run that is stopped closes its
        input and ends straight away, whatever is still going in the
        background, since its whole process group is ended with it.

        Codex's `codex exec` and OpenCode's `opencode run` read a single prompt
        and can't be fed more while they work, so a task running with either
        takes its prompt as ever and can't be sent more.

        Questions, the palette's file search, the one-off runs, and the notes,
        commit messages, and prompt titles each take a single prompt, as ever.

use /lib
from ../project-data import ProjectDataScope
from ../project-directory import ProjectDirectoryScope
from ../prompt-mode/ask-conversation import AskConversationScope
from ../prompt-mode/mode-system-prompts import ModeSystemPromptsScope
from ../prompt-mode/sending import PromptSendingScope
from ../settings-window import SettingsWindowScope
from ../user-preferences import UserPreferencesScope
from ./baked-prompts import BakedSystemPromptsScope
from ./catalog import HarnessCatalogScope
from ./one-off-run import OneOffAgentRunScope
from /scope/container-environment import ContainerEnvironmentScope
from /scope/prompt-mode/chat-input import ChatInputScope
from /ui/components/task-table import TaskTableScope

export scope HarnessIntegrationScope:
    concept: {HarnessIntegrationConcept}

concept HarnessIntegrationConcept:
    pitch:
        Uses the one-off version of a coding harness for the selected
        ${ProjectDirectoryScope}: `claude -p`, `codex exec`, or `opencode run`,
        whichever the user chose. Each run carries on a conversation, so the
        harness keeps its context between requests.

    shape: {HarnessIntegrationShape}

shape HarnessIntegrationShape:
    description:
        Should always run in auto mode.

        The project's system prompt, its system template filled in, as the
        @{ModeSystemPromptsScope} says, is appended to the harness's own
        system prompt, for example with `--append-system-prompt`, the same for
        every prompt of a conversation whatever its mode. The compiled
        systemPrompt of a prompt's hidden anchor, its mode's instructions,
        heads the prompt's own message instead.

        The prompt is given to the harness on its standard input, and what the
        harness does is streamed back as it happens. A task's run takes its
        prompt as a stream of messages rather than a single one, so it can be
        fed more while it works, as its feeding says.

        Its directory, which a system prompt's HARNESS_DIRECTORY stands for,
        is that of the harness in use: .claude, .codex, or .opencode.

        Spec tasks, a Chain prompt's spec steps and spec follow-up, and
        questions always run the harness in a container the application owns,
        as the @{ContainerEnvironmentScope} says, which holds only what their
        mode may use. Every other run, Code tasks and a Chain prompt's code
        step, always, with their protected locations, Freeform, and the
        application's own, runs the harness on the host, in the project directory. Either
        way the harness is run, prompted, and read just as this says.

    harnesses:
        The harness in use is the one picked in the @{SettingsWindowScope}:
        Claude Code, Codex, or OpenCode, Claude Code until another is picked.
        It is remembered for the user, as the @{UserPreferencesScope} says, not
        for a project. Every run the application starts goes to it, the tasks,
        the questions, the palette's file search, the one-off runs, and the
        notes, commit messages, and prompt titles it writes, and everything
        else works the same whichever it is. A run already going when another is picked
        finishes with the harness it started with, and a conversation is only
        carried on by the harness it began with; the next request with another
        harness starts a new one.

        Each harness is run its own way, streaming what it does as a line of
        JSON per event, which is read into the same reply, tool calls, usage,
        and result, whichever harness wrote it:

        - Claude Code is `claude -p`, in auto mode, the system prompt given
            with `--append-system-prompt`, a conversation carried on with
            `--resume`, and a copy of one with `--fork-session`.
        - Codex is `codex exec`, with `--full-auto` and `--json`, the prompt
            read from its standard input, a conversation carried on with
            `resume`.
        - OpenCode is `opencode run`, with `--format json`, a conversation
            carried on with `--session`.

        Codex and OpenCode take no system prompt of their own, so it is given
        ahead of the prompt, marked off from it. Neither can carry on a copy of
        a conversation, so a question asked while another is running starts a
        new conversation with them instead. The notes, commit messages, and
        prompt titles are written with a small model where the harness can be
        told one, Claude Code's haiku, and with the harness's default model otherwise.

        When the harness picked isn't installed, a run on the host fails
        saying that it can't be run, as any run that can't be started does. A
        run in a container uses the harness in its image instead, and fails,
        where Podman isn't installed or can't run, as the
        @{ContainerEnvironmentScope} says.

    protectedLocations:
        Only a run on the host has protected locations. A run in a container
        has none, since nothing it mustn't touch is mounted there, as the
        @{ContainerEnvironmentScope} says: it isn't guarded, and its harness is
        given no rule against reading or editing anything.

        Where the harness takes rules for what its tools may do, as Claude
        Code does with `--disallowedTools`, a run on the host is told what its
        mode keeps it off. A Code task is told it may not edit the spec location, and a
        Spec task the code location; the application puts back whatever
        changes there all the same, and says so in the task's output as a
        passive notice, never an error, as the @{TaskTableScope} says. A Code
        task is also told it may not read the spec location, alongside that,
        so it reads the compiled reference instead, as the
        @{ModeSystemPromptsScope} says. A question from the Ask tab always
        runs in a container, so it is never given this rule, nor any other
        telling it to keep off the spec location. This rule is only a nudge, and
        doesn't enforce anything, since a shell command can still read the
        files, and nothing puts anything back or stops the run when one does. A harness that
        takes no such rules is told nothing of either.

    feeding:
        A task's run is given its prompt as a stream of messages: Claude Code
        with `--input-format stream-json`, each message written as a line of
        JSON on the harness's standard input, which stays open for as long as
        the run lasts. The run's first message is the task's compiled prompt,
        as ever, and each message sent to the task after it, from the
        @{ChatInputScope}, is written as another.

        A message reaches the harness when it finishes what it is doing rather
        than interrupting it, so a run that is mid-tool-call takes it once that
        call is over. The harness echoes each message back as it takes it in,
        with `--replay-user-messages`. A message taken in between turns is
        answered with a result of its own, and one taken while a turn is under
        way is answered within that turn, sharing its result.

        A run can also start work in the background that goes on after its
        turn ends: Claude Code's subagents, shell commands run in the
        background, such as a long build, and any other kind of background
        task it adds later. Every such task holds the run open, whatever its
        kind. The run keeps each background task that has started and not yet
        ended, by its id: one starts when the harness says a task has started,
        and ends when the harness notifies that task's end, whatever it ended
        as. A notification doesn't say what kind of task it is, so it is
        matched by id against those seen starting. The harness wakes the run
        when a background task ends, so it can act on what came of it.

        A result no longer ends the task on its own. The run's last result is
        the first to come once every message sent has been taken in and no
        background task is still going. A result that comes before then, while
        a message sent hasn't been taken in or a background task is still
        going, is only an answer: the task keeps running, its input stays
        open, and more can still be sent to it. At the last result the run's
        input is closed, but the task is only shown as finished once the
        harness's process has exited as well, and it then finishes in the
        state of that last result; until the process exits, the task keeps
        running. A process that exits without a last result finishes the task
        as a run with no result does, failed. A run that is stopped closes its
        input and ends straight away, whatever is still going in the
        background, since its whole process group is ended with it.

        Codex's `codex exec` and OpenCode's `opencode run` read a single prompt
        and can't be fed more while they work, so a task running with either
        takes its prompt as ever and can't be sent more.

        Questions, the palette's file search, the one-off runs, and the notes,
        commit messages, and prompt titles each take a single prompt, as ever.

    images:
        Images attached to a prompt, as the @{ChatInputScope} says, are given
        to the harness as it takes them: to Claude Code as image content blocks,
        base64-encoded with their media type, in the same stream-json user
        message as the prompt's text, after it; to Codex with an `--image`
        argument per image; and to OpenCode with a `--file` argument per image.
        A message fed to a running Claude Code task carries its images the same
        way, and a Claude Code run that isn't fed more but has images is given
        its prompt as a stream-json message too, so the images can go with it.
        Codex's options end with `--` before the prompt when it is given
        images. Questions take images as tasks do.

    context:
        The harness keeps its context between requests instead of starting fresh
        each time. Each lane of the @{PromptSendingScope} carries on a
        conversation of its own, so nothing a task of one lane read reaches a
        task of the other: the spec lane's, carried on by Spec tasks and a
        Chain prompt's spec steps, and the code lane's, carried on by Code
        tasks, a Chain prompt's code step, and Freeform tasks. Each task sent
        carries on its own lane's, and since a lane runs one task at a time,
        two tasks never carry on the same conversation at once. A Chain
        prompt's steps hand on to each other as text, the prompt and what the
        step before replied, as the @{ModeSystemPromptsScope} says, so the
        handoff crosses lanes whatever each lane's conversation holds. When
        the project is opened, each lane carries on the latest conversation
        among its own tasks in the history, a Chain task by the lane of the
        step it was.

        The spec lane and the questions always run in a container, and the
        code lane always on the host, so each conversation is only ever
        carried on where it began. A run in a container keeps its
        conversation's sessions in the project, in its own folder of
        `.suspense/sessions/`, as the @{ContainerEnvironmentScope} says, so
        it carries on across runs, restarts of the application, and moves of
        the project; a run on the host keeps them where the harness keeps
        them on the host.

        Questions from the Ask tab share a separate
        conversation of their own, and when the project is opened they carry on
        the latest conversation among the questions saved with it. A question
        asked while another is running carries on a copy of that conversation,
        so questions running at the same time never write over each other. A
        conversation is only carried on in the project it began in, each open
        project keeping its own tasks' and questions' conversations while it is
        in the background. A spec lane or questions conversation from before
        its sessions were kept in the project, whose session the project's
        sessions folder doesn't hold, is still tried, and when the harness
        has no such session, the request is sent again at once as a new
        conversation, as below.

        A request whose conversation can't be carried on, because the
        harness says it has no such session, as Claude Code's "No
        conversation found", or because it was begun elsewhere, is never
        failed for it, and never retried on the same conversation: it is
        sent again at once as a new conversation, the same prompt, with no
        context, and the conversation it couldn't carry on is not tried
        again by any later request, the project's history included. A
        question sent again so is recorded and shown as starting a new
        conversation, as the @{AskConversationScope} marks one. Each run applies
        its own prompt's systemPrompt, even when it carries on a conversation
        begun in a different mode. The palette's file search always starts
        fresh.

        A conversation can be left for a new one, from the chat input's New
        conversation button, as the @{ChatInputScope} says, which leaves the
        conversation of the lane it is used for: the next request in it
        starts a new conversation with no context, and the one left is not
        carried on again, not by a run of it still going, nor by the project's
        history. Leaving it is kept with the project, as the @{ProjectDataScope}
        says, so a project opened after a lane's or the questions' conversation
        was left starts a new one there too, rather than carrying on the latest
        conversation in its history, until a run after the reset begins one of
        its own. How much context a conversation holds is
        known from what the harness reports with each reply: everything the
        model was given, cached or not, and what it wrote, as of its latest
        reply; replies of subagents don't count.

    failures:
        A run that fails always says what went wrong, in the harness's
        own words, which are the error its result carries, or the error events it
        streamed, and where it gave none, what it printed on its standard
        error, and its exit status, as written. A task shows it in its
        output and a question at the end of its answer. It never reads
        only "the harness reported an error", or any other message that
        leaves the cause unnamed; a generic line is only ever a heading
        above what the harness said. A run that couldn't be started says
        why it couldn't, and one Podman couldn't run says so, as the
        @{ContainerEnvironmentScope} says.

    bakedPrompts: @{BakedSystemPromptsScope}

    oneOffRuns: @{OneOffAgentRunScope}

    catalog: @{HarnessCatalogScope}

    modeSystemPrompts: @{ModeSystemPromptsScope}

use /lib
use /ui
use /ui/components/sidebar/Sidebar
from ./referenced-files import ReferencedFilesPanel
from ./subagents import SubagentsPanel
from ./understanding import UnderstandingPanel
from /scope/application/Body import BodyScope
from /ui/components/scrollbar import ScrollbarScope
from /ui/components/sidebar import SidebarScope

export sidebar RightSidebarScope:
    side: right

    panels:
        - @{ReferencedFilesPanel}
        - @{UnderstandingPanel}
        - @{SubagentsPanel}

    concept: {RightSidebarConcept}

concept RightSidebarConcept:
    pitch:
        A second @{SidebarScope}, at the right of the message list and the
        chat input beneath it, that lists
        the spec files the running task references, so it's clear what part of
        the spec the harness is working from, and the constraints it has taken
        from it for the task.

    shape: {RightSidebarShape}

shape RightSidebarShape:
    description:
        It runs the full height of the body, beside the body's tab bar, the
        message list or file beneath it, and the chat input beneath those, which stops at its left edge rather than
        running beneath it. It keeps the width it was dragged to while the
        application runs.

        Its panels sit one above the other, in this order: the referenced
        files at the top, the understanding beneath them, and the subagents
        last, along the bottom of the sidebar, beneath both. The referenced
        files are only as tall as their rows need, up to half the sidebar's
        height, scrolling beyond that; the subagents, once there are any, are
        only as tall as their rows need, up to 30% of the sidebar's height;
        and the understanding fills what is left between them, until they are
        resized. While the run has started no subagent, the understanding
        reaches the sidebar's bottom.

    resizingPanels:
        The panels themselves can be resized, as the sidebar can. The edge
        between one panel and the next, where the lower panel's header meets
        the body of the one above, is a handle: dragging it up or down moves
        that edge, the panel above growing as the one below shrinks, or the
        other way, their contents laid out anew at each height as it changes.
        Hovering the handle shows the resize cursor for up and down and a thin
        line along the edge in the theme's accent, which goes once the pointer
        leaves and the drag is over; otherwise no line is drawn there, the
        change of colour still being the edge.

        No panel can be dragged shorter than its header and one row of its
        contents, 32 pixels below its header, nor can one be pushed out of
        the sidebar. Once a panel has been dragged, it keeps its height rather
        than being only as tall as its rows need: the referenced files no
        longer fit their rows or stop at half the sidebar, and scroll once
        their rows are taller than the height they were given. The heights
        they were dragged to are kept while the application runs, the next
        time the sidebar slides out included, as its width is; when the
        sidebar's height changes, as when the window is resized, the
        referenced files and the subagents keep their heights and the
        understanding takes what is left, as far as the smallest heights
        allow. Double-clicking the handle puts
        both panels back as they start, the referenced files fitting their
        rows again.

    look:
        The sidebar's body is on the ribbon's command area colour, #222222 in
        dark mode. Each panel's header is 32 pixels tall, on the darkest
        surface, #111111 in dark mode, as the file tree is, its title in
        small semibold text, 8 pixels from the left, with no count beside it.
        There is no line anywhere in it, not between a header and its body,
        nor between one panel and the next: the change of colour is the edge.
        Each header has, along its bottom, the 1 pixel border in its panel
        body's colour that every panel header has, as the @{SidebarScope}
        says, which is no line, since it is the body's own colour.
        The only line is the one down its left edge, where it meets the
        message list and the chat input, which is the handle it is resized
        by, apart from the line that shows along the edge between two panels
        while it is hovered or dragged, as resizing the panels says. In light mode the
        same steps are taken, as the ribbon's are.

        Neither panel has a permanent scrollbar, since its column would break
        the 8 pixel inset: a panel shows its scrollbar only while its contents
        are taller than it, and none otherwise. When it shows, it is the
        same scrollbar as every other, as the @{ScrollbarScope} says.

        A panel whose contents fit doesn't scroll at all, not even by a
        pixel, at any display scale or window size: it counts as taller than
        its contents need only once they overflow it by a whole pixel or
        more, so what is left over from rounding to the display's pixels
        never counts, and while they fit, it stays scrolled to its top. So
        neither the wheel nor a drag moves rows that all fit, and no
        scrollbar shows for them.

    showing:
        It is only there while a task is running: from the moment a task is
        sent from the Code, Chain, or Spec tab until its run is over. Questions
        from the Ask tab never show it, even when one is sent from the queue.

        When a task starts, it slides out from the right edge of the message
        list and the chat input, growing from nothing to its width, its
        contents sliding into view from behind that edge as it does. When the
        run is over, it slides back the same way. The slide is quick and
        settles without bouncing. It pushes rather than covers: from the
        first frame of the slide to the last, the body's tab bar, the message
        list or open file beneath it, and the chat input end exactly at the
        sidebar's left edge, narrowing as it grows and widening as it
        shrinks, laid out again each frame, as the @{BodyScope} says. Nothing
        runs beneath the sliding sidebar, nothing is clipped by it, and
        nothing jumps to a new width once the slide settles.


export ReferencedFilesPanel
export UnderstandingPanel
export SubagentsPanel

export panel SubagentsPanel:
    title: Subagents and commands
    counted: false
    height: fit
    scrolls: true
    scrollbar: overflowing

    concept: {SubagentsConcept}

concept SubagentsConcept:
    pitch:
        The bottom panel of the @{RightSidebarScope}, beneath the referenced
        files and the understanding: the subagents and background commands
        the harness started for the running task, each shown in the colour of
        the mode that started it, with how long it has been running, so one
        that seems stuck can be seen and stopped.

    shape: {SubagentsShape}

shape SubagentsShape:
    description:
        It lists the background tasks the harness started for the run, as the
        @{HarnessIntegrationScope} keeps them: its subagents, the agents it
        started, and its background commands, the shell commands it ran in the
        background, such as a long build. A background task of any other kind
        isn't shown.

        It is shown only once the run has started one, and takes no room
        before. One row per background task, in the order they started,
        subagents and commands together, each 24 pixels tall, 8 pixels in
        from the panel's edges: a spinner while it is at work, then a tick, a
        cross, or a dash for how it ended, done, failed, or stopped, beside a
        small icon for its kind, a robot for a subagent and a terminal for a
        command, in the theme's muted grey, then what it was started to do, in
        small text, cut off with an ellipsis, muted once it has ended. For a
        subagent that is its description, and for a command the command
        itself, on one line, in monospace. Its tooltip gives what it was
        started to do, and beneath, muted, its kind, "Subagent" or "Command",
        and what it is doing or how it ended. The panel is only as tall as its
        rows need, up to 30% of the sidebar's height, scrolling beyond that.

    elapsed:
        At the right of each row, 8 pixels in from the panel's edge, is how
        long it has been running, from when the harness said it started, in
        extra small muted tabular figures, as a task's elapsed time is written
        beside its status: "0:42", "12:05", "1:02:33". While it is at work it
        counts up every second; once it has ended it stops at how long it ran.
        What it was started to do is cut off before the time rather than
        running beneath it.

    stopping:
        A row at work can be stopped, from a Stop button: a small ghost button
        with a stop icon, 18 pixels square, which takes the place of its
        running time while the row is hovered, whose tooltip reads "Stop this
        subagent" or "Stop this command". Clicking it stops only that
        background task, as the @{HarnessIntegrationScope} says: the task the
        run is for and every other background task carry on, and nothing else
        in the panel or the task's output changes. Once clicked, the button
        is disabled and the row's spinner stays until the harness notifies its
        end, when it shows a dash for stopped, as any stopped one does. A row
        that has ended has no Stop button, and neither does one whose run
        can't stop it on its own, as one whose input is already closed, where
        the task's own Cancel button stops everything still going.

    byMode:
        Each background task is shown according to the mode of the task that
        started it, as the @{PromptModesScope} colours modes: its row has a
        bar 2 pixels wide down its left edge in that mode's colour, and its
        spinner and tick are drawn in it too, while a cross or dash keeps its
        own colour. A background task's mode is the mode its task was sent
        in, and for a step of a chain, the step's own: the spec step and a
        spec follow-up are Spec's, and the code step is Code's, never Chain's
        purple. Its tooltip names the mode, "Started by the Code task",
        "Started by the Spec step", and so on. A task whose mode isn't known,
        as one from the history saved before modes were, has no bar and keeps
        its spinner and tick in their own colours, its tooltip reading
        "Started by the task". A Chain task on its own, before its code step
        has been sent, is the chain's spec step, so its background tasks are
        Spec's and labelled "Spec".

        While a chain runs, the panel keeps the background tasks of each of
        its steps, not only the step running: they are grouped by step, in
        the order the steps ran, each group headed by a small label in its
        mode's colour, "Spec", "Code", or "Spec follow-up", with the step
        running last. A task that isn't part of a chain has one group, and no
        label. Once the run is over, the sidebar slides back with them all,
        as it says.
EOF

        small icon for its kind, a robot for a subagent and a terminal for a
        command, in the theme's muted grey, then what it was started to do, in
        small text, cut off with an ellipsis, muted once it has ended. For a
        subagent that is its description, and for a command the command
        itself, on one line, in monospace. Its tooltip gives what it was
        started to do, and beneath, muted, its kind, "Subagent" or "Command",
        and what it is doing or how it ended. The panel is only as tall as its
        rows need, up to 30% of the sidebar's height, scrolling beyond that.

        long it has been running, from when the harness said it started, in
        extra small muted tabular figures, as a task's elapsed time is written
        beside its status: "0:42", "12:05", "1:02:33". While it is at work it
        counts up every second; once it has ended it stops at how long it ran.
        What it was started to do is cut off before the time rather than
        running beneath it.

        A row at work can be stopped, from a Stop button: a small ghost button
        with a stop icon, 18 pixels square, which takes the place of its
        running time while the row is hovered, whose tooltip reads "Stop this
        subagent" or "Stop this command". Clicking it stops only that
        background task, as the @{HarnessIntegrationScope} says: the task the
        run is for and every other background task carry on, and nothing else

        is disabled and the row's spinner stays until the harness notifies its
        end, when it shows a dash for stopped, as any stopped one does. A row
        that has ended has no Stop button, and neither does one whose run
        can't stop it on its own, as one whose input is already closed, where
        the task's own Cancel button stops everything still going.

    byMode:
        Each background task is shown according to the mode of the task that
        started it, as the @{PromptModesScope} colours modes: its row has a
        bar 2 pixels wide down its left edge in that mode's colour, and its
        spinner and tick are drawn in it too, while a cross or dash keeps its
        own colour. A background task's mode is the mode its task was sent
        in, and for a step of a chain, the step's own: the spec step and a
        spec follow-up are Spec's, and the code step is Code's, never Chain's
        purple. Its tooltip names the mode, "Started by the Code task",
        "Started by the Spec step", and so on. A task whose mode isn't known,
        as one from the history saved before modes were, has no bar and keeps
        its spinner and tick in their own colours, its tooltip reading
        "Started by the task". A Chain task on its own, before its code step
        has been sent, is the chain's spec step, so its background tasks are
        Spec's and labelled "Spec".

        While a chain runs, the panel keeps the background tasks of each of
        its steps, not only the step running: they are grouped by step, in
        the order the steps ran, each group headed by a small label in its
        mode's colour, "Spec", "Code", or "Spec follow-up", with the step
        running last. A task that isn't part of a chain has one group, and no
        label. Once the run is over, the sidebar slides back with them all,
        as it says.
